bib.title: Beyond Individual Intelligence: Surveying Collaboration, Failure Attribution, and Self-Evolution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Beyond Individual Intelligence: Surveying Collaboration, Failure Attribution, and Self-Evolution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems", Qi, Ma, Xing, Guo, Huang et al. (Xi'an Jiaotong Univ. and others), arXiv 2605.14892v2 (cs.AI), 15 May 2026, preprint survey. Local file: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/03-agentic-foundations/sources/qi-2026-beyond-individual-intelligence.pdf

COVERAGE: 316,295 chars in total. I read chars 0-236,000 (all body text, tables, Sections 1-6) in full. The rest (about 80k chars) is the reference list. I skimmed it only to resolve citation numbers for specific claims. There are no appendices. The extraction was clean text. Table cell values extract as flat text, so columns are sometimes hard to line up.

FIT WARNING: This is a taxonomy and literature-map survey. It reports NO experiments and NO quantitative synthesis of its own, and it has no equal-compute comparison between multi-agent and single-agent setups. For 04b (when more agents pay at equal compute) it adds only one sentence that points to another paper. That paper is Kim et al. 2025, "Towards a science of scaling agent systems", arXiv:2512.08296, ref [341]. Cite Kim et al. directly and do not cite this survey for the claim. The survey is more useful for 04 (patterns and taxonomy) and for the failure-taxonomy part of 04b, where it cites Cemri et al. (MAST). I did not read Kim et al. or Cemri et al. The survey gives no numbers for either.

CLAIMS (ranked; the survey makes no measurements, so every claim is the authors' synthesis)
1. Claim: Adding agents does not guarantee better performance, and communication overhead and interference grow non-linearly, so expansion gives diminishing returns.
   number: none
   setup: One-line assertion in the Section 3.6 and 5.1 discussions. No data given. Attributed to Kim et al. 2025 [341], arXiv:2512.08296.
   quote: "Increasing the number of agents does not guarantee better performance [341]." and "Communication overhead and the risk of interference grow non-linearly [341]."
   where: Section 3.6 (p.39, about char 141,500); Section 5.1 (p.52, about char 190,000)
2. Claim: Errors in tightly coupled MAS propagate and cascade, and the point where a failure shows up often differs from where it began.
   number: none
   setup: Qualitative synthesis. Primary sources: Cemri et al. 2025 "Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?" [20], arXiv:2503.13657; Ma et al. 2025 [342] and [353] (FailCycle).
   quote: "the point at which an anomaly becomes observable often does not coincide with its true origin, and final failure is frequently the product of multiple interacting stages rather than a single isolated error"
   where: Section 4.5.1, p.49 (about char 176,000)
3. Claim: General-purpose long-context LLMs are weak at locating the responsible agent and step in failure traces, and incomplete observability makes this worse.
   number: none
   setup: The authors' reading of Who&When (Zhang et al., ICML 2025 [344]), TRAIL (Deshpande et al. 2025 [28]) and TraceElephant (Chen et al. 2026 [345]).
   quote: "both TRAIL [28] and TraceElephant [345] show that general-purpose long-context models remain limited in debugging complex execution trajectories and that incomplete observability further undermines attribution quality."
   where: Section 4.3.1, p.42 (about char 159,500)
4. Claim: Sequential pipelines give coherence but propagate early errors. Parallel pipelines give diversity and robustness but make aggregation expensive when outputs conflict. The authors expect the best systems to combine both.
   number: none
   setup: Design-trade-off discussion. Parallel examples cited: self-consistency [64], multi-agent debate (Du et al. 2024 [306]), Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al. 2025 [307]).
   quote: "Sequential pipelines encourage coherence but risk error propagation, since early mistakes constrain downstream reasoning. Parallel pipelines improve diversity and robustness but may create expensive aggregation problems when candidate outputs conflict."
   where: Section 3.6, p.38 (about char 140,500)
5. Claim: Heterogeneous roles beat homogeneous ones on complex tasks, but they add interdependence, interface mismatch, cascading errors and coordination overhead. Homogeneous teams are said to get stuck in "repeated self-consistency loops".
   number: none
   setup: Qualitative. Supporting papers: X-MAS (Ye et al. [209]; the text cites it as [212]) and A-HMAD (Zhou and Chen 2025 [213]), cited as improving results. The "self-consistency loops" statement is attributed to [208], which is Zhong et al. 2024 "Heterogeneous-agent RL" (JMLR). That is an odd attribution, so check it before reuse.
   quote: "As role diversity increases, so does interdependence among agents, making the system more sensitive to interface mismatches, cascading errors, and coordination overhead."
   where: Section 3.6, p.37 (about char 135,500); Section 3.1.1, p.26
6. Claim: No orchestration topology is universally best. Centralized gives control but creates a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Distributed gives robustness but makes consensus hard. Hybrid is the trend, and topology should be chosen per task.
   number: none
   setup: Based on the Table 7 framework comparison (12 frameworks, none benchmarked head to head).
   quote: "no orchestration topology is universally superior."
   where: Section 3.6, p.38 (about char 138,500)
7. Claim: Explicit natural-language communication is costly. It adds token overhead and latency, and it can amplify inconsistency. Implicit or latent communication is proposed as an alternative.
   number: none
   setup: Opinion. Cited: AgentPrune "Cut the crap" (Zhang et al., ICLR 2025 [253]), LatentMAS [264].
   quote: "Repeated broadcasting of long textual states creates token overhead, increases latency, and can amplify inconsistency when agents interpret shared context differently."
   where: Section 3.6, p.38
8. Claim: The survey states that nobody knows when specialization or extra agents help, because dynamic-role systems use heuristics. This is the survey's own admission of the gap that 04b addresses.
   number: none
   setup: Section 3.6 discussion.
   quote: "many current systems implement dynamic roles heuristically, but do not yet learn when specialization is necessary, when redundancy is beneficial, or when additional agents simply add noise."
   where: Section 3.6, p.38
9. Claim: Quantified result from the self-evolution section: Optima gets a 2.8x performance gain with 90% fewer tokens. AFlow lets small models beat GPT-4o at 4.55% of inference cost. MaAS surpasses state of the art at 15% of the compute cost.
   number: 2.8x / 90%; 4.55%; 15%
   setup: Secondhand figures. The survey gives no benchmark or baseline details. Primary sources: Optima (Chen et al., Findings of ACL 2025 [386]); AFlow (Zhang et al., ICLR 2025 [149]); MaAS (Zhang et al. 2025 [410], arXiv:2502.04180). Verify in the originals before citing.
   quote: "achieving a 2.8 × performance gain while reducing token usage by 90%"; "enabling small models to outperform GPT-4o at 4.55% of inference cost"; "surpassing state-of-the-art at 15% of computational cost"
   where: Section 5.3.1 p.55; Section 5.3.3 p.58
10. Claim: Attribution benchmarks are small and mostly manual, and attribution definitions are inconsistent, so method results cannot be compared directly.
   number: Who&When 184 cases; TRAIL 148; AgentFail 307; AgentErrorBench 200; CORRECT-Error 2000+; AgentErrata 210; MP-Bench 289; TraceElephant 220
   setup: Table 9 (p.47) lists these dataset sizes. The survey reports no accuracy numbers.
   quote: "Who&When [344] Localization 184Manual Agent+Step+Interp. FL Accuracy" and "method-level performance is difficult to compare directly"
   where: Table 9, p.47; Section 4.5.1, p.49

TAXONOMY IN BRIEF
- Overall frame is "LIFE": Lay individual capabilities, Integrate through collaboration, Find faults through attribution, Evolve through self-improvement.
- Formal MAS tuple S = (A, E, C, G, Π): agents, environment, communication protocol, orchestration topology, collaboration policies.
- Collaboration has four axes (Sec. 3):
  - Role. Capability is homogeneous or heterogeneous. Allocation is static or dynamic.
  - Communication. Mode is explicit or implicit. Protocols are internal (A2A, ANP, ACP, Agora) or external (MCP, LMOS, Agent Protocol); see Table 6.
  - Orchestration. Centralized, distributed or hybrid. Routing sits inside the topology.
  - Interaction. Information flow is sequential or parallel. Pattern is cooperative or competitive.
- Failure taxonomies (Sec. 4.2), three families:
  - System structure: Pan/Cemri's three groups (specification and design; inter-agent misalignment; verification and termination), and AgentAsk's four communication failures (Data Gap, Referential Drift, Signal Corruption, Capability Gap).
  - Execution stage: TRAIL's three groups (reasoning; system execution; planning and coordination).
  - Causal lifecycle: AgentFail's three levels (agent, workflow, platform).
- Failure attribution is formalized as (I,t) = f(Ω,τ,q) when Z(τ)=1. Methods are data-driven, constraint-guided or causal-inference.
- Self-evolution has three loci: agentic (prompt, memory, parameters), systemic (topology, composition, shared memory) and meta (knowledge space or generator).
- Single-agent capabilities (Sec. 2) are reasoning, memory, planning, and tool use.
- Note: the survey does NOT use the common pattern names (supervisor/worker, handoff, evaluator-optimizer, debate, swarm). Debate, MoA, planner-executor and hierarchical map loosely onto its parallel, cooperative/competitive and hybrid categories.

LIMITS
- No experiments, no pooled results and no equal-compute analysis. Claims on when collaboration helps or hurts are qualitative.
- The authors concede that the failure-taxonomy literature has "no widely accepted unified framework". Most attribution methods assume a single cause and single effect. Data realism and annotator agreement are weak. Attribution is not yet tied to repair.
- The authors concede that "no orchestration topology is universally superior", and that scalability, reliability and cost are open.
- It covers work to roughly early 2026. Several cited items are 2026 arXiv preprints, and I could not check them.
- Some citation mapping looks sloppy: [212]/[209] for X-MAS, and the same arXiv ID 2509.23735 given for both [342] and [353]. Do not trust a number or attribution without checking the primary paper.
- Its claim that homogeneous teams "get trapped in repeated self-consistency loops" is weakly sourced, since [208] is an RL paper. Do not repeat it as established.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
Figure 4, p.24: "Overview of the multi-agent collaboration system... a three-tiered design framework comprising the Foundation, Structure, and Execution layers to categorize agent roles, communication modes, orchestration topologies, and interaction dynamics". It is the single-page map of the Role / Communication / Orchestration / Interaction taxonomy, and would suit note 04. Runner-up: Figure 6 or 7, p.40/47, on failure attribution, for 04b. I did not run the figures script; the caption text is copied from the extraction.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- Figures are not extracted as text. Figure 5's text contents came through as garbled fragments.
- Table columns are flattened and some checkmarks are ambiguous.
- Nothing here can support a "multi-agent vs single agent at equal compute" claim from this source. Going to Kim et al. (arXiv:2512.08296) and Cemri et al. (arXiv:2503.13657) directly is the right step.
